title: India Cracks Down on GLP-1 Weight-Loss Drugs With Supply Chain Sweep
excerpt: India's drug regulator has inspected 49 entities and banned surrogate advertising of semaglutide-based weight-loss drugs as cheap generics flood the market after patent expiry.
body:
• India's Drugs Controller has audited 49 entities — including online pharmacies, wholesalers, and wellness clinics — for unauthorized GLP-1 drug sales.
  • The CDSCO banned all surrogate advertising of semaglutide products, including influencer campaigns and branded disease-awareness content.
  • Only endocrinologists, internal medicine specialists, and cardiologists may prescribe the drugs; violators face licence cancellation and prosecution.
  • The crackdown follows semaglutide's patent expiry in India, which triggered a wave of generics priced 50–80% below Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy.

India's top drug regulator has launched a nationwide enforcement drive against the unauthorized sale and promotion of GLP-1 receptor agonist weight-loss drugs, conducting audits at 49 entities and banning all forms of surrogate advertising as a flood of cheap generics reshapes the market.

The Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), operating under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), said inspections in recent weeks targeted online pharmacy warehouses, drug wholesalers, retail pharmacies, and wellness and slimming clinics across multiple regions, according to a statement from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Notices have been issued to entities found in violation.

Generics Trigger a Market Rush

The crackdown follows the expiry of Novo Nordisk's semaglutide patent in India in March 2026, which prompted at least seven domestic pharmaceutical companies — Sun Pharma, Dr Reddy's, Alkem, Torrent, Cipla, Zydus Lifesciences, and Glenmark — to launch generic versions of the blockbuster GLP-1 drug. These generics are priced 50 to 80 percent below Novo Nordisk's branded Ozempic and Wegovy, according to LiveMint.

India's semaglutide market is projected to reach approximately $347.5 million by 2035, growing at a compound annual growth rate of nearly 18 percent, according to a CareEdge report. A Lancet study projects the number of overweight and obese adults in India will rise from 180 million in 2021 to 449 million by 2050, making the country the world's second-highest burden of obesity after China.

Surrogate Advertising Banned

On March 10, 2026, the CDSCO issued a comprehensive advisory to all manufacturers, explicitly prohibiting surrogate advertisements and any form of indirect promotion that could mislead consumers or encourage off-label usage. The ban covers print, television, digital, and social media platforms.

"Any promotional activity that functions as a surrogate advertisement for prescription-only drugs shall be viewed seriously and may be treated as irrational or misleading marketing practice."

— CDSCO advisory, March 2026

The advisory specifically calls out influencer engagement, corporate campaigns, and awareness-led activations that build brand recall for prescription products. Communications suggesting guaranteed weight-loss outcomes, exaggerating therapeutic benefits, or undermining lifestyle interventions such as diet and exercise are prohibited. Companies have been directed to audit all live campaigns, influencer contracts, and content partnerships, and to file a Risk Management Plan covering ongoing safety monitoring.

Prescription Restricted to Specialists

The government reiterated that semaglutide has been approved in India on the condition that it is prescribed only by endocrinologists, internal medicine specialists, and — for some indications — cardiologists. The Health Ministry warned that non-compliance would be met with "cancellation of licenses, penalties, and prosecution under applicable laws."

"It's a very essential step to ensure the drug gets used by the right patients. Excessive and improper use carries a real risk of complications like gall bladder stones, risk of dehydration and protein malnutrition."

— Dr Monika Sharma, Senior Endocrinologist, Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi

Earlier DCGI raids on wellness centres had revealed the drug was being pushed by individuals without super-specialty qualifications, according to LiveMint. Health authorities have flagged potential side effects ranging from nausea and vomiting to pancreatitis, kidney injury, and bowel obstruction.

What's Next

The government said regulatory surveillance will continue to intensify in the coming weeks. With India's generic drug industry rapidly expanding access to semaglutide, the regulator's enforcement push is a direct attempt to ensure the market's growth does not outpace safety guardrails. For now, the message to the pharmaceutical industry and consumers alike is clear: GLP-1 drugs remain prescription-only medications that demand specialist oversight.
